aliases: the Holy Spirit (as promised in the Gospel of John)

summary: The Paraclete (Greek parakletos, rendered in English as Advocate, Comforter, Helper, or Counselor) is the title Jesus gives the promised Holy Spirit in the farewell discourse of the Gospel of John (chapters 14-16). Jesus says that he will ask the Father, who will send 'another Paraclete' in Jesus's name to be with his disciples forever, the Spirit of truth who will teach them all things, bring his words to their remembrance, testify to Jesus, and be sent only after Jesus departs. In mainstream Christian tradition the Paraclete is identified with the Holy Spirit, the third person of the Trinity. This entry reports the Johannine sayings and their interpretation as the tradition's account, without adjudicating it.
description:
'Paraclete' is the English form of the Greek parakletos, a word from the legal and personal sphere meaning one called alongside (para-kletos) to help, and so an advocate, intercessor, helper, or comforter. In the New Testament the noun is distinctive to the Johannine writings: it appears as a title of the promised Spirit in the farewell discourse of the Gospel of John and, applied to the risen Christ himself, once in 1 John 2:1. The range of English renderings (Advocate, Comforter, Helper, Counselor) reflects the difficulty of carrying the single Greek term into English, and different translation traditions have chosen differently: the King James Version reads 'Comforter', the English Standard Version 'Helper', and the New Revised Standard and several modern versions 'Advocate'.

The Paraclete sayings cluster in John 14-16 and are read verbatim here. In John 14:16-17 Jesus says, in the King James rendering, 'And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever; Even the Spirit of truth', whom the world cannot receive. In John 14:26, 'But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you.' In John 15:26, 'But when the Comforter is come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me.' And in John 16:7, 'It is expedient for you that I go away: for if I go not away, the Comforter will not come unto you; but if I depart, I will send him unto you', continuing (16:8-14) that the Paraclete will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment, will guide the disciples into all truth, and will glorify Jesus by taking what is his and declaring it. The passages thus present the Paraclete as another advocate alongside and after Jesus, sent by the Father in Jesus's name and by the departing Son, whose work is to teach, remind, testify, convict, and guide.

In mainstream Christian tradition, across the Fathers and the later confessions, the Paraclete of the Johannine discourse is identified with the Holy Spirit, the third person of the Trinity, and the 'proceeds from the Father' of John 15:26 became a key text in the later filioque debate over the procession of the Spirit. Two further readings are recorded here strictly as attributed positions, not as fact and not adjudicated. First, the second-century New Prophecy (Montanism), on the report of its hostile heresiological opponents, is said to have claimed that the Paraclete spoke through Montanus; the Anonymous quoted by Eusebius (Ecclesiastical History 5.16) reports the movement's followers 'boasting that Montanus was the Paraclete'. Second, Islamic tradition has read the parakletos of John, sometimes connected with a proposed reading periklytos ('praised', 'illustrious'), as a foretelling of the prophet Muhammad, associating it with the Qur'anic name Ahmad (Qur'an 61:6); this is an Islamic interpretation, which Christian tradition does not accept, and the two readings are set side by side here without ranking or harmonizing them.
editorial_notes:
This entry describes the Paraclete on the Christian tradition's own terms (neutrality #6): the Johannine sayings are reported and the mainstream identification of the Paraclete with the Holy Spirit, third person of the Trinity, is given as the tradition's account, not adjudicated by the editor (neutrality #1). The range of English renderings (Advocate, Comforter, Helper, Counselor) is presented as a translation matter, with no single rendering privileged as the only correct one.

TWO CROSS-TRADITION AND CONTESTED READINGS ARE HANDLED AS STRICTLY ATTRIBUTED (neutrality #1, #2, #11). (1) The Montanist claim that the Paraclete spoke through Montanus is reported only as the testimony of the movement's hostile opponents (the Anonymous quoted by Eusebius, EH 5.16, 'boasting that Montanus was the Paraclete'), not as fact and not as the movement's adjudicated self-understanding. (2) The Islamic reading of parakletos/periklytos as a foretelling of Muhammad (linked to the name Ahmad, Qur'an 61:6) is recorded as an ATTRIBUTED Islamic interpretation and is NOT adjudicated; it is explicitly noted that Christian tradition does not accept it. Per neutrality #11 this cross-tradition note states the shared text and the difference of reading and does not rule which reading is correct; the compares_with relation to the Islamic reading names the shared question (what/whom the Johannine parakletos foretells) and the difference, and ranks neither. No polemic of either tradition against the other is used as a neutral description of the other.

Sourcing triangulates the three Christian lenses per neutrality #8: (a) academic scholarship on the Johannine Paraclete (Raymond E. Brown's study and Gospel commentary, the standard critical treatment of the Paraclete sayings); (b) the primary corpus, the Johannine verses themselves (John 14:16-17, 14:26, 15:26, 16:7-14), read verbatim; (c) a contemporary theologian on Johannine pneumatology (Gary M. Burge, The Anointed Community). No encyclopedias, no Wikipedia, no tertiary sources.

CONFIDENCE HONESTY: this entry is verified-eligible. The load-bearing primary source, the Johannine Paraclete verses, was read verbatim at biblehub.com and the wording confirmed word for word in the King James and ESV renderings (John 14:16 'another Comforter/Helper'; 14:26 'the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost ... he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance'; 15:26 'when the Comforter is come ... he shall testify of me'; 16:7 'It is expedient for you that I go away ... the Comforter will not come unto you; but if I depart, I will send him unto you'); rated high. The Eusebius witness for the Montanist claim was likewise read verbatim at newadvent.org (EH 5.16, 'boasting that Montanus was the Paraclete'), rated high for what the open page reports. Brown and Burge (proprietary) are rated medium, verified to exist and be on-topic but not read line by line. This entry is referenced by montanus and by holy-spirit. The compares_with note on the Islamic reading (islam-view-of-jesus) is included only as a strictly attributed cross-tradition note.

relations.note: In mainstream Christian tradition the Paraclete of the Johannine discourse is identified with the Holy Spirit, the third person of the Trinity; John 15:26 ('proceedeth from the Father') became a key text in the later filioque debate over the procession of the Spirit. Reported as the tradition's account, not adjudicated.
The Paraclete is the title Jesus gives the promised Holy Spirit in John 14-16, whom the Father sends in Jesus's name to teach, remind, and testify.

On the report of the Anonymous quoted by Eusebius (EH 5.16), the followers of the second-century New Prophecy were 'boasting that Montanus was the Paraclete'; the movement's claim of continuing revelation through the Paraclete is central to it as its hostile opponents describe it. Attributed to the hostile source, not stated as fact. This entry supplies the paraclete referenced by montanus.

Shared question: what or whom the Johannine parakletos foretells. Christian tradition reads the Paraclete as the Holy Spirit; an Islamic interpretation reads parakletos, sometimes as periklytos ('praised'), as a foretelling of the prophet Muhammad, linked to the Qur'anic name Ahmad (Qur'an 61:6). The two readings are set side by side as attributed positions; Christian tradition does not accept the Islamic reading, and neither reading is adjudicated or ranked here (neutrality #10, #11). Dangling forward reference; islam-view-of-jesus is not yet a separate entry.

historical_period.note: The Paraclete sayings belong to the farewell discourse of the Gospel of John, conventionally dated to the late first century CE (c. 90-110). The term parakletos and its interpretation as the Holy Spirit have a continuous history in Christian tradition thereafter; the second-century Montanist claim and the later Islamic reading are noted at their own periods. Dates are conventional and mark the textual origin, not a single fixed point.
